article.title: Why More Features Can Make a Model Worse

paragraphs.en: Adding more features to a machine-learning model feels like adding more information. Sometimes it improves prediction, but additional variables can also make a model less reliable. One problem is noise. A feature may look related to the target in the training sample simply by chance. Flexible models can learn that accidental pattern, producing better training metrics but weaker future performance. Leakage is more dangerous. A variable may contain information created after the prediction time, making validation unrealistically easy. Multicollinearity can also make some models unstable or make explanations difficult when several variables carry nearly the same signal. Another risk is a fragile proxy. A system code, campaign flag, or operational status may predict outcomes because of a temporary business process rather than a stable customer relationship. When that process changes, the feature loses meaning. Feature selection should therefore consider more than incremental AUC. Analysts should ask whether a variable is available at scoring time, stable across periods, understandable, legally and ethically usable, inexpensive to maintain, and robust to missing data. Time-based validation can reveal features that work only in one historical period. Ablation tests can show whether removing a feature group materially changes performance. Regularization can reduce statistical overfitting, but it does not solve leakage or poor data governance. Operational cost matters too. A tiny accuracy gain may not justify an expensive data feed or complex real-time aggregation. Simpler feature sets can be easier to monitor and reproduce. The goal is not to minimize the number of features mechanically. Rich information can be valuable when it is stable and genuinely available. The goal is to maximize useful signal relative to noise, fragility, and cost. A production model should be judged by how reliably it supports decisions over time, not by how many columns enter the training table. Analysts should define the population, time window, operational constraint, and decision objective before interpreting the metric.
